title: Espresso & fast promotions
topic: Correlation vs causation and truncated chart axis
blurb: An HR memo tries to prove office espresso machines double your promotion odds.
prompt: An AI drafted this internal HR pitch for buying expensive espresso machines. Spot the two reasoning flaws.

segments.label: Claim 1
segments.text: We analyzed badge swipes and café receipts from 800 employees over the past year.

segments.label: Claim 2
segments.text: Staff who bought 3+ espressos a day at the office café were promoted more often than remote or tea-drinking staff.

segments.label: Claim 3
segments.text: Therefore, drinking more office espresso directly boosts employee performance and causes faster promotions.

segments.label: Claim 4
segments.text: In our summary bar chart (y-axis starting at 48% and ending at 52%), the espresso group's bar (51%) is three times taller than the other group's bar (49%), proving a massive 3× promotion advantage.

segments.label: Claim 5
segments.text: Installing free espresso bars on every floor will triple company-wide promotion readiness.

conclusion: Verdict: Espresso drives a 3× jump in promotions, so free espresso bars will transform productivity.

flaws.original: This shows an association, not causation — confounding factors like working longer on-site hours or holding client-facing roles could drive both café visits and promotions.
flaws.corrupted: Therefore, drinking more office espresso directly boosts employee performance and causes faster promotions.

diagnosis_choices.label: Confuses correlation with causation: confounders (like in-office visibility or long hours) may drive both café receipts and promotions.
Badge swipes cannot be matched to receipts for groups of 800 people.
Tea contains caffeine too, so tea drinkers must always get promoted faster.
Observational data can never show a correlation between two variables.

fix_choices.label: State only a correlation and control for confounders (office attendance, role, tenure) instead of claiming coffee causes promotions.
Raise the threshold from 3 espressos to 5 espressos to prove causation.
Drop remote workers from the dataset and keep claiming espresso causes promotions.
Claim that promotions cause people to hate tea.

flaws.explanation: Observing that frequent café buyers get promoted more often does not mean caffeine caused the promotion. Employees spending long hours in the office or meeting clients on-site both buy more café drinks and get higher visibility.
flaws.why_tempting: Coffee is associated with alertness, so a plausible story makes the leap from 'associated with' to 'causes' feel effortless.
flaws.catch_rule: When a study says 'people who do X get more Y, therefore X causes Y', immediately hunt for a hidden third factor causing both.
flaws.hint: Could a third variable explain both why someone visits the office café often and why they get promoted?

practice.problem: Cities with more fire trucks have more fire damage. Does buying fewer fire trucks reduce fire damage?
practice.answer: No — larger fires cause both more damage and more fire trucks to be dispatched.

flaws.original: Starting the bar chart's y-axis at 0% shows 51% vs 49% — only a 2-percentage-point difference, nowhere near a 3× advantage.
flaws.corrupted: In our summary bar chart (y-axis starting at 48% and ending at 52%), the espresso group's bar (51%) is three times taller than the other group's bar (49%), proving a massive 3× promotion advantage.

diagnosis_choices.label: Truncated y-axis trick: cropping the axis at 48% makes a tiny 51% vs 49% gap look 3× taller visually.
Bar charts are not allowed to display percentages; only pie charts can.
51% is actually smaller than 49% when adjusted for sample size.
The y-axis should end at 1000% to compare two groups.

fix_choices.label: Anchor bar charts at 0% and report the actual ratio (51% vs 49%, a +2 percentage-point gap, ~1.04×).
Crop the y-axis even tighter (48.5% to 51.5%) to make the difference clearer.
Remove axis labels completely so the bars speak for themselves.
Convert the bar chart into a 3D pie chart.

flaws.explanation: Bar height encodes magnitude relative to zero. Starting the axis at 48% makes `51 - 48 = 3` look three times bigger than `49 - 48 = 1`, even though 51% vs 49% is just a 2-point difference (1.04×).
flaws.why_tempting: Readers glance at bar heights and repeat the visual ratio ('3× taller!') without checking where the axis starts.
flaws.catch_rule: Always check the baseline of a bar chart: if the y-axis doesn't start at 0, bar-height ratios are meaningless.
flaws.hint: Compare the actual numbers 51% and 49% against the claimed '3× advantage'.

practice.problem: A bar chart starts at 90% and shows Brand A at 96% and Brand B at 92%. How many times taller is A's bar, vs the real ratio?
practice.answer: The bar looks 3× taller (6 vs 2), while the real difference is only 4 percentage points (96/92 ≈ 1.04×).

clean_segments: We analyzed badge swipes and café receipts from 800 employees over the past year.
Staff who bought 3+ espressos a day had a 51% promotion rate vs 49% for others.
This small correlation does not prove espresso causes promotions, because in-office presence and role mix confound the comparison.
On a zero-based bar chart, 51% vs 49% is only a 2-percentage-point gap (about 1.04×), not a 3× jump.
Espresso bars may be a nice perk, but the data does not show they drive promotions.
clean_conclusion: The data shows only a tiny 2-point correlation with clear confounders, not a 3× causal boost.
